paragraphs.heading: What quartz is
paragraphs.text: Quartz is a hard mineral made of silica, which is silicon dioxide. Its atoms are joined in a continuous framework of SiO₄ tetrahedra, units of silicon and oxygen. Each oxygen atom is shared between two tetrahedra, and that gives the overall formula SiO₂. Among the minerals and mineral groups of Earth's lithosphere, quartz is the second most common, at about 12% by mass. It also defines the value 7 on the Mohs scale of hardness, a scratch method for judging how hard a material is.

paragraphs.heading: The mineral once taken for ice
paragraphs.text: The Ancient Greeks called quartz krustallos, meaning 'crystal', a word derived from kruos, 'icy cold'. Some philosophers, Theophrastus among them, believed the mineral was a form of supercooled ice. The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder also believed quartz was ice, frozen permanently after great lengths of time. He pointed out that quartz turns up close to Alpine glaciers and not in warm climates. The idea lasted until at least the 17th century.

paragraphs.heading: The 60° rule
paragraphs.text: In the 17th century Nicolas Steno studied quartz, and his work paved the way for modern crystallography. He found that the long prism faces of a quartz crystal always meet at a perfect 60° angle, whatever the size or shape of the crystal. This established the law of constancy of interfacial angles.

paragraphs.heading: Two forms and a sudden switch
paragraphs.text: Quartz comes in two forms: α-quartz, the normal one, and β-quartz, the high-temperature one. The change from one to the other happens abruptly at 573 °C at ambient pressure. β-quartz is unstable at room temperature, so any quartz at room temperature is α-quartz, whichever form it started as. The switch needs only a comparatively minor rotation of the tetrahedra relative to one another, and the way they are linked does not change. Even so, the volume changes significantly. That can cause microfracturing in ceramics while they are fired, in ornamental stone that has been through a fire, and in crustal rocks exposed to high temperatures.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of a quartz crystal
paragraphs.text: The ideal quartz crystal is a six-sided prism that ends at both tips in six-sided, pyramid-like rhombohedrons. In nature, crystals often fall short of this. They may be twinned, distorted, or so intergrown with neighbouring crystals that only part of the shape shows, or no obvious crystal faces at all. Well-formed crystals typically grow as a druse, which is a layer of crystals lining a void, and quartz geodes are particularly fine examples. These crystals are attached at one end to the rock around them, and only one pyramid end is present.

paragraphs.heading: Where the colours come from
paragraphs.text: Pure quartz is colourless and transparent or translucent, and is traditionally called rock crystal or clear quartz. Coloured varieties are common, among them amethyst, citrine, rose quartz, smoky quartz and milky quartz. The colours arise from impurities. These alter the molecular orbitals, which leads to electronic transitions that absorb energy from the visible spectrum. The wavelengths that are not absorbed pass through and give the mineral the colour we see.

paragraphs.heading: Crystals too small to see
paragraphs.text: Quartz varieties were once sorted by how visible their individual crystals are. In macrocrystalline varieties the crystals can be seen with the unaided eye. Microcrystalline varieties are aggregates of tiny crystals that only a microscope shows, and in cryptocrystalline varieties the crystals are too small to see even with an optical microscope. Today the last two are commonly grouped together and called chalcedony. Chalcedony is commonly translucent to opaque, whereas macrocrystalline quartz tends to be more transparent.

paragraphs.heading: Electricity from pressure
paragraphs.text: Quartz crystals have one more property. They are piezoelectric, which means they develop an electric potential when mechanical stress is applied to them.
